name: PRP under eyes

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is made by drawing a person's blood and spinning it to concentrate platelets. Clinics offer it under the eyes for thin, crepey or dark skin, promoted for wrinkles and fine lines, aiming for thicker, smoother-looking under-eye skin.

Platelets carry growth factors and cytokines, and proponents propose these support tissue repair and skin quality. Wikipedia describes PRP evidence as mixed and condition-specific. No published trial of PRP specifically for under-eye skin was found, and a registered trial in the nasojugal fold (tear trough) was withdrawn.

paras: Clinics inject it under the eyes or apply it after microneedling, usually as a series of sessions. Preparation methods vary by kit and facility, and results are judged over weeks as skin quality changes.

Adverse effects are generally low in trials. The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, and clinic use is considered off-label. In 2024 the CDC reported HIV cases linked to an unlicensed spa that reused contaminated equipment.

angle.text: Users get PRP injections under the eyes to improve thin, crepey or dark skin, drawing on clinic marketing for wrinkles and fine lines. Growth factors from your own platelets are thought to support skin repair and thickness. Eye-specific trial data is limited.

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a concentrate of plasma from a person's own blood, produced by centrifugation, that retains platelets and the growth factors they carry.[1] Under the eyes, clinics and enthusiasts use it with the aim of improving thin, crepey or dull skin and the hollow, tired look of the tear trough, sometimes pairing it with microneedling in what is marketed as a vampire facial.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes the evidence for PRP as mixed and condition-specific, with stronger support for some wound types and weaker findings for several musculoskeletal uses.[1] A dermatology review summarises current applications of PRP in skin, and a 2025 split-face trial compared PRP with adipose stem cell exosomes for photoaged facial skin.[3][4] A registered trial of PRP in the nasojugal folds (tear trough) was withdrawn, and no published trial specific to under-eye skin was found.[5]
On looksmax.org, members post about PRP and vampire facials as a skin-quality and anti-aging measure and discuss pairing it with biofillers made from platelet-rich fibrin for the tear trough.[6][7]
infobox: Intradermal or subdermal injection, sometimes with microneedling
Preparation devices cleared; clinical use off-label[1]

paras: Blood is spun in a centrifuge to remove red cells while keeping platelets, which carry growth factors that may support tissue healing.[1] Preparation varies between facilities and kits, so results can differ.[1] Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) is a related preparation that forum members describe as a natural filler.[7]

Clinics promote PRP for wrinkles, fine lines, blemishes and hair loss.[1] Vampire facials, which often combine PRP with microneedling, grew popular in the 2010s.[1] A review of PRP in dermatology covers its current skin applications.[3] A 2025 investigator-blinded split-face trial compared adipose-derived stem cell exosomes with PRP on photoaged facial skin.[4] A meta-analysis found PRP studied in alopecia as well.[8]

A looksmax.org member posted about completing a first PRP session and microneedling it into his face, saying he hoped to age less, and other members reacted with surprise.[6] Another thread describes a member planning monthly vampire facials and PRF biofiller in areas including the tear trough, and other members responded with questions about trying it.[7] Preparing and applying PRP at home is a practice some forum members describe; it is not covered here, and clinics offer the treatment under medical supervision.

Adverse effects are generally low across trials, and one review found weak evidence of harm at similar rates in treated and untreated people.[1] In 2024 the CDC reported HIV cases among clients of an unlicensed New Mexico spa that reused contaminated equipment.[1]

No studies found for under-eye PRP specifically. A registered trial of PRP administration in the nasojugal folds (NCT03255681) was withdrawn.[5] A completed phase 2/3 study (NCT01461785, n=25) evaluated PRP in fat transfer, a related but different use.[9] Controlled studies of PRP in other settings include a meta-analysis in alopecia[8] and a split-face trial in photoaged facial skin.[4]

lore.intro: PRP and PRF come up in looksmax.org threads as skin-quality and tear-trough tools, including do-it-yourself setups.[6][7]
